cues.text: Removing every name may still reveal the person.
Which other details should you replace?
You don't replace everything. Keep the useful structure for your task
but remove details the task doesn't need.
You can now turn what you
spotted into a safer working copy.
Remove unnecessary details, replace needed identities with placeholders
or reduce needless precision.
Start with direct identifiers: names, account numbers
email addresses, phone numbers, and street addresses.
Check indirect clues because combinations of exact dates and locations,
with rare roles or unusual events may identify someone.
Removing only the name isn't reliable.
Could someone familiar with the context still recognise the person?
Preserve the original and work on a fresh
copy so mistakes don't destroy your reliable source.
This practice record is entirely fictional and its names, contact details
account identifier, and delivery situation describe nobody real.
For this delivery update, the item and both dates matter
identity and location details don't.
I replace the fictional name with
the role-labelled greeting placeholder [CUSTOMER_NAME].
The account identifier isn't needed
so I delete its entire line.
The assistant won't deliver anything
so I delete the email and street address too.
The unneeded concierge instruction could narrow the location
so I remove it.
I keep both delivery dates because they explain the change
limiting exposure without losing task-relevant information.
If location mattered, I could generalise an apartment to a residential building
here, no location is needed.
Number same-role placeholders consistently.
CUSTOMER_1 and CUSTOMER_2 preserve who did what without exposing either identity.
A placeholder isn't anonymous if a separate list links it to someone. Keep any lookup key protected
separate, and out of the prompt.
The sanitised source retains one role placeholder, the item, and both relevant dates.
I removed the account, contact, and precise location.
Before copying, read the sanitised version alone. Could someone complete the draft?
Does it contain any detail they don't need?
I place the sanitised information in a clear request. Separating the task, source
constraints, and output makes each part easy to check.
The input states the writing goal and only the necessary facts,
it never suggests that the assistant can search for missing personal information.
The constraints preserve placeholders, use only supplied facts, label missing information
and prevent sending; this separates drafting from external action.
The requested output is a subject line and brief message; it doesn't request realistic names
account values, or invented reasons for the delay.
Only this sanitised request goes to the assistant,
the original practice record stays local because the task doesn't need that extra information.
The response is generated material. It isn't opened evidence or a sent message.
That matters because fluent wording doesn't confirm the underlying facts.
The greeting keeps CUSTOMER_NAME instead of inventing a person.
The subject and opening also preserve the item and original date from the sanitised source.
The main sentence keeps the new estimate and asks for confirmation.
It doesn't give a reason for the delay because none was supplied.
The assistant marks the missing sender name with another placeholder.
That's safer than filling the gap with a realistic but unsupported identity.
I compare the draft with the sanitised source. First
every placeholder must stay unchanged so an invented name can't enter the final message.
Second, I match the item and both dates, character by character.
Those details came from the fictional source, not the generated explanation.
Third, I confirm that no removed details returned. The draft has no account identifier
email address, street address, or concierge instruction.
Finally, I check for invented actions or outcomes. The message doesn't claim the delivery was booked, confirmed, or sent
because none of that happened.
I return the checked draft to a local working document. If real values are genuinely required
add them there under your normal access and review controls.
Before any real use, verify the intended recipient, dates, attachments, and remaining placeholders. The assistant provided the wording
but you still control approval and sending.
If you can't verify that the redaction is safe, upload nothing. Recreate only the necessary context in a fresh local template
using placeholders from the start.
This manual route may take longer, but it keeps an uncertain source file on your device.
A safer example can still preserve the task.
Sanitising text for an AI prompt and redacting a file for distribution are related but different tasks.
A safe prompt copy doesn't prove the file is safe.
A highlight, white box, or black shape may only hide what you see. If you'll share the file
use a genuine redaction operation that removes the content.
A file you distribute may also contain metadata, comments, tracked changes, hidden text, or embedded content.
Replacing visible details with placeholders doesn't inspect those areas.
Save the redacted result as a new file. Reopen it, then test that the removed text is gone. Search for it
and where appropriate, select and copy content to confirm nothing remains accessible.
Editing the original shared cloud document may leave earlier values in its version history. Create a separate, sanitised artifact.
Don’t assume visible deletion erased earlier versions.
Before sharing a sanitised artifact, check the intended recipient, assigned access role, and general-access setting. Interface names may vary
so verify these controls in your account.
The principle stays the same, whatever tool or device you use. On a phone, computer, or document assistant
provide only the minimum useful context.
The same method works for messages, notes, forms, and sample records. Keep roles, relationships, the order of events
and task facts. Remove identity clues you don’t need.
Use four questions for a quick redaction check. What can you remove? What needs a placeholder?
What can you make broader? Does the task still make sense?
For practice, make a safer copy of a fictional reminder or service note.
Keep only enough context to draft a clear update.
Your finished practice set should show the fictional source, sanitised input, generated draft, and checking result. If you’re unsure about the redaction
demonstrate the manual fallback instead.
The goal isn’t to make every example vague. Preserve its purpose with the smallest suitable amount of information,
and make sure a person deliberately checks the result.
In the next lesson, I’ll show you how to review history, sharing, and data settings.
You’ll learn what your account may retain or expose.
Keep the task context, remove identity details you don’t need, and check what remains. If you’re unsure it’s safe
create a fresh example using placeholders only.
Thank You for watching. I am EMMANUEL CORELS. See you in the next video.
